title: Does AI Adoption Drive Economic Growth? Cross-National Evidence from Emerging Economies
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely expected to raise productivity, yet whether its diffusion is already lifting growth in emerging economies is unclear. We assemble a panel of 42 emerging economies over 2010–2023 and construct an AI Adoption Capacity Index (AACI) that combines five indicators of connectivity, compute and data infrastructure, competency and technological context through principal component analysis. The index is validated against AI patenting (Spearman ρ = 0.59). Two-way fixed-effects growth regressions with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors find no positive short-run association between the AACI and GDP per capita growth: the preferred estimate is −1.07 percentage points per standard deviation (p = 0.12). System GMM estimates are negative and significant, but their over-identification diagnostics are marginal, and a peer-diffusion instrument is too weak to be informative. The average hides systematic heterogeneity. The AACI’s growth effect rises with tertiary enrolment (interaction p = 0.02), and it is more negative in economies with below-median initial income. Using Penn World Table data, total factor productivity and labour productivity growth respond negatively in the short run. Together, these patterns match a productivity J-curve, in which building AI capacity absorbs resources before complementary skills and intangibles pay off. They do not support the view that AI capacity is already a growth engine for emerging economies. The results caution against treating AI infrastructure as a substitute for human-capital deepening and point to absorptive capacity as the binding constraint on AI-led convergence.
